we-the-people-1787-1791.works: The blue and orange-red pies and the size legend make Virginia stand out at a glance. Each pop-up has the state's name in the title and every number the three-fifths fill-in needs (19, 22, 13) in one place. The Spanish sheet gives the English layer and bookmark names with a Spanish gloss, so my students can find House seats in 1793 and Ratifying the Constitution in Map layers.

findings.where: Population in 1790 pop-up (q1-virginia picture); Q1 'Who lived where in 1790?' step 3 (read the percentage in the first line) and the 'more than a quarter' answer
findings.what: The first line says '292,627 of them enslaved (39.099998474121094%)'. My students will stop at that long number. Several of mine learned decimals with a comma at school, so a sixteen-digit number with a point in it is a real puzzle, and the question already asks them to turn 'una cuarta parte' into 25%.
findings.why: The one number Q1 needs is buried in digits that mean nothing. My English learners spend their reading effort decoding it, and some will copy it whole or misread it.
findings.suggestion: Round the percentage in the pop-up to a whole number or one decimal (for example '39%'), using the pop-up's number formatting or Round() in its expression.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q1-virginia.png; pop-up text '1790 census: 747,610 people, 292,627 of them enslaved (39.099998474121094%).'

findings.where: Population in 1790 / House seats in 1793 pop-up (q1-virginia and q2-seats); Q3 'The three-fifths clause' step 2 ('the last two lines' / 'las dos últimas líneas')
findings.what: The sheet says the full-count and no-count seats are in the last two lines, but they're in the third paragraph. The last lines are the note about Kentucky or Maine and 'Seats: National Archives · Ratio: U.S. Census Bureau'. In the Virginia picture the box is cut off at that note, so a student who scrolls to the bottom as the step says finds sources, not seats.
findings.why: My English learners follow steps word for word. When a step sends them to the wrong place, they copy the wrong line or give up on the fill-in.
findings.suggestion: Change step 2 in both sheets (and the matching step on the lesson page) to point to the paragraph that starts 'If enslaved people had been counted in full'; in Spanish: 'luego el párrafo que empieza con If enslaved people had been counted in full (si se hubiera contado a todas las personas esclavizadas)'. Or move that paragraph to the end of the pop-up so 'the last two lines' becomes true.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q1-virginia.png, we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png; pop-up text, third of five paragraphs: 'If enslaved people had been counted in full: 22 seats. If they had not been counted at all: 13 seats.'

findings.where: All pop-ups and labels on this map; the Spanish sheet's steps in Q1 to Q4
findings.what: The Spanish steps say escaños, esclavizadas, libres, a favor, en contra, Carolina del Sur and Carolina del Norte. The pop-ups say 'House seats', 'enslaved', 'for', 'against' and 'South Carolina in 1790', and the labels say 'SC' and 'NC'. To my students 'seats' means asientos. Nothing on the sheet tells them that escaños = seats, or which English words to look for.
findings.why: My students find a number in an English pop-up by spotting the English word for it. Without that word they have to read every line.
findings.suggestion: In the Spanish sheet, put the English word in brackets the first time each key term appears, or add a small word box under Cómo leer el mapa: escaños (seats), esclavizadas (enslaved), libres (free), censo (census), a favor (for), en contra (against), contadas por completo (counted in full), Carolina del Sur (South Carolina, SC), Carolina del Norte (North Carolina, NC).
findings.evidence: Pop-up text in q1-virginia, q2-seats and q4-nc ('19 House seats in 1793', '194 for, 77 against'); labels 'SC 8' and 'NC 12' in we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png

findings.where: Ratifying the Constitution pop-up for North Carolina's second pie (q4-nc); Q4 step 3 (read the votes in the first line) and step 4 and 'Why does North Carolina have two pies?'
findings.what: The first line is 'Ratified on 11/21/1789, 12:00 AM: 194 for, 77 against.' The votes come last, after a date in US order and a midnight time that means nothing. My students schooled in Mexico or Central America put the day first, so a date like 2/6/1788 reads to them as 2 June. Then the note says the first convention 'voted 184 to 83 against ratifying', the reverse of 'X for, Y against', so 184 can be read as the votes for.
findings.why: Q4 is about comparing votes for and against. The pop-up makes my students work through a date and a reversed sentence before they reach the numbers.
findings.suggestion: Put the vote first and write the date out with no time: '194 for, 77 against. Ratified November 21, 1789.' Word the note in the same pattern: 'A first convention, at Hillsborough in 1788, did not ratify: 83 for, 184 against.'
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-nc.png; pop-up text 'Ratified on 11/21/1789, 12:00 AM: 194 for, 77 against.' and 'A first convention, at Hillsborough in 1788, voted 184 to 83 against ratifying.'

findings.where: Ratifying the Constitution at the opening extent (q4-ratify); Q4 steps 3 and 4 and 'Which three votes were closest?'
findings.what: From New York to New Hampshire the pies pile on top of each other. Some labels are missing (I can't find MA, CT, NJ or DE), and 'RI 13' is printed beside the biggest pie, which must be Massachusetts. Those are the close votes the question is about. The app has a New England and New York bookmark, but the sheet never sends students to it.
findings.why: The map has no place names, so my students rely on the labels. Here the labels point them to the wrong pie, and the closest votes are the hardest pies to click.
findings.suggestion: Add a step to Q4 in both sheets, before clicking the pies: 'Open the New England and New York bookmark' / 'Abre el marcador New England and New York (Nueva Inglaterra y Nueva York)'.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png

findings.where: House seats in 1793 labels shown together with Ratifying the Constitution pies and labels (q2-seats), and population pies together with ratification pies (q4-nc); Q2 step 2 (read the labels) and 'Your answer' (evidence from two layers)
findings.what: The seats picture shows two kinds of label at once: 'VA: 19' and 'NY: 10' (seats), and 'VA 10', 'MD 7' and 'PA 2' (the order of ratifying). Only a colon tells them apart. The population pies and the ratification pies also use the same blue and orange-red for different things: free and enslaved, and for and against.
findings.why: My students read the picture before the words. 'MD 7' looks like Maryland's seats, and an orange-red slice could mean enslaved people or votes against. When they combine layers for the final answer, they'll mix up the meanings.
findings.suggestion: Make the ratification labels clearly an order ('VA 10th' or 'VA #10'), or put the word in the seat labels ('VA 19 seats'). Give the ratification pies a different pair of colors (for example green for ratify, purple for against). Also check why the ratification pies and labels show in the q2 picture when the legend lists only House seats and Population.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png, we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-nc.png

rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-liv.works: The district pop-up is one short sentence with the name in bold and the party in brackets ('Mike Carey (Republican) represents Ohio Congressional District 15'), which my students can read and copy. The Topographic basemap has real place names, so they can find their own town. The Spanish sheet glosses building, district and site for the legend.

findings.where: National Register of Historic Places pop-up (q4-nrhp-click); Reading the map ('Its pop-ups give an address but not a name' / 'dan una dirección, pero no un nombre') and Q4 'History where we live' step 3
findings.what: The pop-up's title says 'Ohio Statehouse' in bold. The sheet tells my students there is no name, and sends them to a basemap label or to the National Archive Information link, which is a long English record. Also, the diamond that opened 'Ohio Statehouse' seems to sit south of downtown near the Brewery District, not at High and Broad by the Columbus label, so 'the label under the diamond' would name something else.
findings.why: The sheet contradicts the screen. My students trust the sheet, so they'll ignore the name in front of them and do the hardest reading in the lesson.
findings.suggestion: Change both sheets: 'The pop-up title gives the place's name' / 'El título de la ventana emergente da el nombre del lugar'. Keep the National Archive link as an extra. Hide the 'National Register Information Tracking System Reference Number' line, which repeats the Property ID. Check where the Ohio Statehouse point sits.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp-click.png; pop-up text 'Ohio Statehouse / Property ID: 72001011 / SE corner of High and Broad Sts.'; compare the diamond's position with rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png

findings.where: Topographic basemap building labels; Q2 'Rights in public places' steps 1 and 2, Q3, and Q4's answer (courthouse, post office, school, library)
findings.what: The Spanish sheet lists tribunal, ayuntamiento, biblioteca, lugar de culto, centro de votación and redacción de un periódico. The basemap labels will be in English: Courthouse, City Hall, Library, Church, Post Office. None of these are cognates, and 'Library' looks like librería, a bookshop. Also, at the street-level zoom in the historic-places picture, the basemap shows streets, parks and neighborhoods but no building names yet.
findings.why: My students can't find a place they can't recognize in English. They'll zoom around looking for 'biblioteca' or 'tribunal'.
findings.suggestion: In the Spanish sheet, put the English map word after each place: tribunal (Courthouse), ayuntamiento (City Hall), biblioteca (Library), iglesia u otro lugar de culto (Church, Temple, Mosque, Synagogue), oficina de correos (Post Office), escuela (School). In step 1 add 'keep zooming in after the street names appear' / 'sigue acercándote después de que aparezcan los nombres de las calles'.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png (no building names at street-level zoom); Spanish sheet Q2 step 2

findings.where: Congressional districts at the opening view (open); Q1 'Who represents us?' step 4 and 'How many districts does your state have?'
findings.what: Zoomed out, every district line is the same thick blue, the state borders disappear under them, and no state names show. To count, my students would have to pick out small shapes without seeing where their state ends.
findings.why: Counting depends on seeing the state's edge, and the pop-up doesn't help: it gives the district's number, not how many districts there are. In Columbus the district number (15) happens to match Ohio's total, which invites the wrong method.
findings.suggestion: Add a state-boundary layer drawn darker or thicker than the district lines, or add a short second line to the pop-up such as 'Ohio has 15 districts.'
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png; q1-district pop-up text

findings.where: National Register of Historic Places legend and diamonds (q4-nrhp); Q4 step 4 (use the legend to tell a building from a district or a site)
findings.what: In the legend, district (brownish red) and site (dark red) look alike, and structure (pale yellow-green) almost disappears on the light basemap. The diamonds on the map are tiny. The pop-up already says 'Resource Type: building' in words.
findings.why: Telling apart two dark reds on tiny symbols is hard for anyone. The word in the pop-up is easier, and the Spanish sheet already glosses it.
findings.suggestion: Change step 4 in both sheets to 'Read Resource Type in the pop-up' / 'Lee Resource Type (tipo de recurso) en la ventana emergente: building (edificio), structure (estructura), district (distrito), site (sitio), object (objeto)'. On the map, make the diamonds larger and give district and site more different colors.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png; pop-up text 'Resource Type: building'

findings.where: The Tip under Cómo leer el mapa (same on all five Spanish sheets in this group); pop-up footers in q4-nrhp-click ('1 of 2'), war-of-1812 q2-neworleans ('1 of 2') and louisiana-purchase q3-biomes ('1 of 3')
findings.what: The Spanish tip says the pop-up will say '1 de 2'. On the map it says '1 of 2', small, in the bottom corner next to two arrows. Here every click on a diamond also catches the district underneath, so students will see it every time.
findings.why: My students look for the exact words the sheet gives them. If they don't see '1 de 2', they won't know to use the arrows.
findings.suggestion: On every Spanish sheet: 'Si la ventana emergente dice 1 of 2 (1 de 2) abajo, usa las flechas < > para ver cada elemento.'
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp-click.png; war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q2-neworleans.png; louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biomes.png

presidential-elections-1796-1800.works: Each pop-up title gives the state and its electors exactly as the sheet promises ('Pennsylvania: 15 electors'), and the 'In the pie' sentence links the two colors to two names. The orange and blue are easy to tell apart. Zoomed in, the two pink squares, their labels and Maryland's pie sit clearly apart for Measure.

findings.where: Landmark Supreme Court cases, Marbury v. Madison square (q4-marbury); Q4 'The Supreme Court, near the capital' steps 1 and 2 and 'What happened in each place?'
findings.what: Clicking the Marbury v. Madison square opened nothing. My students get the McCulloch pop-up and its Why here part, but have nothing to read for Marbury.
findings.why: Half of Q4 can't be answered from the map, and my students have no English text to work from for that case.
findings.suggestion: Open the Marbury square in the live map. Check that its pop-up is enabled and its expression doesn't fail, and that no layer without a pop-up (such as the District of Columbia outline) sits on top of it. Fix it so it opens like McCulloch's.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q4-marbury.png; pop-up text '(no pop-up opened)'

findings.where: Landmark Supreme Court cases squares over the Election of 1796 pies at The sixteen states view (open, q1-pie, q4-mcculloch); Q1 step 3 (click each two-color pie, including Maryland) and Q4 steps 1 and 3 (click the squares, Measure)
findings.what: At the opening view the two pink squares sit on top of Maryland's two-color pie and on each other, and only the Marbury label shows. Clicking Maryland may open a court case instead of the vote. Q4 never tells students to zoom in, although the lesson page does. Zoomed in, as in the Marbury picture, the squares, labels and Maryland's pie are clearly apart.
findings.why: My students will click the pie and get a court case in dense legal English, and measuring between two overlapping squares gives a meaningless distance.
findings.suggestion: Add to Q4 step 1 in both sheets: 'Zoom in on Maryland until the two squares are apart' / 'Acércate a Maryland hasta que los dos cuadrados se separen', or add a bookmark for the capital area. In Q1, remind students to use the pop-up arrows if a court case opens. Or set the cases layer to draw only when zoomed in closer than The sixteen states.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--open.png, presidential-elections-1796-1800--q1-pie.png, presidential-elections-1796-1800--q4-marbury.png

findings.where: Election of 1800 turned on and Election of 1796 off, with a pop-up open (q2-1800); Q2 'The election of 1800' and Q3 'Which states switched?' (switching layers)
findings.what: After the switch to 1800, the Pennsylvania pop-up still shows 'Electors' votes in 1796'. The title, 'Pennsylvania: 15 electors', is the same for both years, so the year appears only inside the first line. In the same picture New York's pie is olive green and Pennsylvania's looks mixed. Those colors aren't in the legend; it looks as if the 1796 pies are still showing through.
findings.why: Q2 and Q3 are about comparing the two years. My students will copy 1796 numbers as 1800 numbers. New York is the answer to Q3, and it shows a color that the legend can't explain.
findings.suggestion: Put the year in each pop-up title ('Pennsylvania in 1800: 15 electors'). Add to Q2 and Q3 in both sheets: 'Close the pop-up before you switch layers' / 'Cierra la ventana emergente antes de cambiar de capa'. Check that turning 1796 off removes its pies completely and that the pie symbols are opaque, so overlapping pies never blend into colors that aren't in the legend.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q2-1800.png (pop-up first line 'Electors' votes in 1796' with the 1800 legend showing; olive New York pie)

findings.where: McCulloch v. Maryland pop-up (q4-mcculloch); Q4 step 2 (read the Why here part) and 'What happened in each place?'
findings.what: The Why here part is a single sentence, which is good, but it depends on 'sued', 'cashier', 'branch' and 'tax'. The rest of the pop-up is heavy: 'charter', 'unconstitutional and void', 'appropriate means', 'the power to tax involves the power to destroy'. The Spanish sheet glosses only 'Why here'.
findings.why: My students can find the Why here part, but they can't say what happened without those four words.
findings.suggestion: Add a word box to Q4 on the Spanish sheet: sued (demandó), cashier (cajero), branch (sucursal), tax (impuesto), bank (banco), commission (nombramiento), ruling (fallo). Optionally use plainer words in the Why here line, for example 'worked at the Baltimore office of the Bank of the United States'.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q4-mcculloch.png; pop-up text 'Why here: Maryland sued James McCulloch, a cashier at the Baltimore branch of the Bank of the United States, to collect a state tax on the bank.'

findings.where: Election of 1796 pop-up (q1-pie); Q1 step 3 (read each two-color pie's pop-up)
findings.what: The first line lists four names (Adams 1, Jefferson 14, Pinckney 2, Burr 13), though the pie shows only two. The second paragraph sorts this out but says 'John Adams (Federalist), 1 votes'.
findings.why: My students copy sentences from pop-ups as models for their answers, and four names before the two that matter add reading for no gain.
findings.suggestion: Fix the plural ('1 vote') in the pop-up expression, and put the 'In the pie' sentence before the full list of candidates.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q1-pie.png; pop-up text 'Electors' votes in 1796: John Adams 1, Thomas Jefferson 14, Thomas Pinckney 2, Aaron Burr 13.' and 'In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), 1 votes'

louisiana-purchase-1803-1806.works: The yellow Louisiana Purchase next to the 1783 land shows 'about double' at a glance, and the purchase pop-up puts both fill-in numbers in one sentence. The Across the Rockies bookmark clearly shows the trail leaving the yellow, with the Pacific Northwest unshaded. The watershed pop-up gives the region's name in large type, and 'Region' is a cognate.

findings.where: Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail and Lewis and Clark campsites (approximate), in every view (open, q1-purchase, q2-watersheds, q4-rockies); Reading the map ('A purple line' / 'Una línea morada'), Q3 step 2 and Q4 step 2
findings.what: The sheet and legend promise a purple line. On the map I see a thick chain of orange-red dots. The purple shows only in a few gaps in Idaho and Montana and between dots west of the Rockies.
findings.why: My students match the color words on the sheet to the screen. 'Línea morada' matches nothing they can see, so they'll wonder whether they turned on the right layer.
findings.suggestion: Draw the trail above the campsites and make it thicker, and make the campsite symbols smaller or hollow, or show them only when zoomed in. Or change the sheet to 'a line of orange-red dots (campsites) over a thin purple line (the trail)'.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--open.png, louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q1-purchase.png, louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q4-rockies.png

findings.where: Lewis and Clark campsites east of where the trail ends (q1-purchase, q2-missouri-basin, q3-biome-click); Q4 'Across the Rockies' steps 3 and 4 (find Pittsburgh, Measure)
findings.what: The map has no place names, so 'Pittsburgh' is only 'the trail's eastern end'. Three pictures show loose campsite dots farther east, toward Maryland and Virginia, beyond the end of the line of dots. A student looking for the eastern end will start from the last dot.
findings.why: The measurement could fall outside 2,100 to 2,300 miles, and there's no label my students can read to check they are at Pittsburgh.
findings.suggestion: Add one labeled point for Pittsburgh (or a label at the trail's start), or reword step 3: 'the eastern end of the trail line, where the Ohio River begins, not the separate dots farther east' / 'el extremo este de la línea, donde nace el río Ohio, no los puntos sueltos más al este'.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q1-purchase.png, louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q2-missouri-basin.png, louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biome-click.png

findings.where: Up the Missouri bookmark with Biomes on and the legend open (q3-biomes); Q3 'Up the Missouri' steps 3 and 4 (turn off Watersheds, turn on Biomes, click the shading and read the first line)
findings.what: In this view I see no biome colors: only the yellow purchase, the brown watershed outlines and a cyan selected area. Clicking along the route opened 'Souris-Red-Rainy Region, HUC ID: 09, States touched by this HUC: …', marked 1 of 3. A student who reads the first line, as step 4 says, will write a watershed as the biome. Zoomed out (q3-biome-click), the biome colors and the biome pop-up work.
findings.why: My students would copy an English name they can't recognize as wrong. The step only works if Biomes actually draws here and Watersheds is really off.
findings.suggestion: Check that Biomes draws at the Up the Missouri bookmark's scale (its visible range) and above Territorial acquisitions, and that turning off United States Watersheds hides all its HUC sublayers. Or set the bookmark one zoom level out. Add to step 4: 'If the pop-up shows a Region, use the arrows to find the biome' / 'Si ves una Region, usa las flechas para buscar el bioma'.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biomes.png; pop-up text 'Souris-Red-Rainy Region / HUC ID: 09' (1 of 3); compare louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biome-click.png

findings.where: Territorial acquisitions to 1803 when a feature is selected (q1-purchase; also the Missouri Region selection in q2-missouri-basin); Q1 'A bigger country' steps 2 and 3
findings.what: When a student clicks the Louisiana Purchase, the yellow turns bright green with a cyan edge. That puts two greens on the map, and the sheet's whole comparison is yellow against green.
findings.why: My students rely on the color words in the sheet. While they read the pop-up, the purchase looks like the 1783 land.
findings.suggestion: Change the app's selection highlight to one that doesn't turn yellow into green (for example a dark outline with no fill), or add to step 3: 'The area turns green while it is selected; close the pop-up to see the yellow again' / 'La zona se ve verde mientras está seleccionada; cierra la ventana para ver el amarillo otra vez'.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q1-purchase.png, louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q2-missouri-basin.png

findings.where: Opening view with the legend open (open); Q1 step 1 ('Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark and use the legend') and step 2 (compare yellow with green)
findings.what: With the legend open, the panel covers most of the green 1783 land. My students would compare the whole yellow area with a strip of green.
findings.why: They'll underestimate the 1783 land and get 'about how much bigger' wrong.
findings.suggestion: Set The Louisiana Purchase bookmark so the 1783 land sits to the left of the legend panel, or add to step 2: 'Read the legend, then close it to compare' / 'Lee la leyenda y luego ciérrala para comparar'.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--open.png

findings.where: Biomes legend and pop-up (q3-biomes, q3-biome-click); Q3 'Which biome covers the Great Plains?'
findings.what: The answer is 'Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands', in English, and the Spanish sheet doesn't translate it. Below it, 'Nature Could Recover' is a paragraph about protected habitat that the question doesn't need. In the legend, Mangroves and Temperate Grasslands are almost the same khaki. The map has no labels, and 'Great Plains' (Grandes Llanuras) is not explained anywhere.
findings.why: Without a gloss my students copy the name without knowing it means grassland, so they can't use it to explain why the Corps followed rivers.
findings.suggestion: In the Spanish sheet, gloss 'Temperate Grasslands (pastizales templados)' and 'Great Plains (Grandes Llanuras: the flat grassland the Missouri crosses)'. Trim the pop-up to the biome and ecoregion lines, or hide the Nature Could Recover section. Change one of the two khaki legend swatches.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biome-click.png (pop-up text 'Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands … Nature Could Recover …'); louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biomes.png (legend)

findings.where: United States Watersheds layer (HUC 2s to 12s, all on inside the group); Spanish sheet's Cómo leer el mapa and Q2 'Why New Orleans?' step 2
findings.what: The English sheet says Watersheds shows larger regions when you zoom out and smaller ones when you zoom in. The Spanish sheet leaves that sentence out. If students click while zoomed in, they'll get '1 of 2' or more with smaller basins, and only the answer notes say to pick the one whose HUC ID has two digits.
findings.why: My students reading the Spanish sheet won't know why the outlines change, and won't know which of several pop-ups is the region they need.
findings.suggestion: Add to the Spanish sheet: 'United States Watersheds muestra regiones más grandes al alejarte y más pequeñas al acercarte.' Add to Q2 in both sheets: 'If it says 1 of 2, use the one whose HUC ID has two digits, like 10' / 'Si dice 1 of 2, usa la que tiene un HUC ID de dos cifras, como 10'.
findings.evidence: Spanish and English sheets, Reading the map; louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q2-missouri-basin.png pop-up text 'Missouri Region / HUC ID: 10' (one pop-up at this zoom; the stacking when zoomed in is inferred)

war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine.works: The battle pop-up gives the date written out in words, the winner and the casualties in three short lines before the long story, so my students can answer Q2 without reading the narrative, and 'January 8, 1815' is easy to compare with December 24, 1814. The treaty-line pop-ups are one short sentence each, and on the Latin America bookmark the blue circles and orange diamonds are easy to tell apart.

findings.where: Battles of the War of 1812 pop-up (q2-neworleans); Q1 'Where was the war fought?' (name three areas)
findings.what: The pop-up gives the battle's name, date, winner and casualties, but no state or region. The lesson page says to read 'State Name' in the pop-up, and it isn't there. With no state names on the map, my students must name 'the Great Lakes', 'Chesapeake Bay' and 'the Gulf Coast' in English, and nothing on the map gives them those words. Under the top lines the story runs to four long paragraphs, and the last one is printed twice.
findings.why: My students can see the three clusters but can't name them, and the extra text makes the box scroll for nothing.
findings.suggestion: Add the state at the top of the pop-up ('New Orleans, Louisiana', or a 'State:' line) and remove the repeated paragraph. Give a word bank for Q1 in the Spanish sheet: Grandes Lagos (Great Lakes), frontera con Canadá (Canadian border), bahía de Chesapeake (Chesapeake Bay), costa del golfo de México (Gulf Coast).

findings.where: Battles legend 'Total Casualties' and battle pop-ups (q1-bookmark, q2-neworleans); Adams–Onís Treaty line pop-ups (q3-treatyline); Reading the map, Q2, and Q3 step 4
findings.what: The Spanish sheet says 'bajas', but the legend and pop-ups say 'Casualties', which my students will read as casualidades (coincidences). The size legend also ends at '< 0'. On the treaty line, part 1 is clear ('The Sabine River, from the Gulf of Mexico north to latitude 32° N'), but the answer notes show that later parts use phrases like 'upstream to its source', which the sheet doesn't explain.
findings.why: A false friend in the legend title changes what my students think the diamond sizes mean, and the border question depends on reading direction words in English.
findings.suggestion: In the Spanish sheet: 'bajas (casualties: muertos, heridos, desaparecidos y prisioneros)', plus a word box for Q3: river (río), upstream (río arriba), source (nacimiento), north along / west along (hacia el norte por / hacia el oeste por), latitude (latitud), longitude (longitud). Change the smallest legend class from '< 0' to '0' or a real low value.
findings.evidence: Legend text in q1-bookmark ('Total Casualties … < 0'); war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q2-neworleans.png ('Total Casualties: 2,096'); war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-treatyline.png

findings.where: The 1819 boundary bookmark with Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line on and the legend open (q3-boundary); Q3 'Florida and a new border' steps 3 and 4
findings.what: In this view Florida, the main green land, is behind the legend at the right edge. The only green I can see is a small patch near the source of the Arkansas River in the Rockies. The line's first parts (the Sabine, and north to the Red River) are also behind the panel, and the Land Spain gave up in 1819 legend entry shows no swatches here.
findings.why: My students follow 'Haz clic en la tierra verde' literally. They'll click the small patch in the Rockies, miss Florida, and skip the first parts of the line.
findings.suggestion: Reset The 1819 boundary bookmark so Florida and the Gulf end of the line sit to the left of the legend (center it farther east, or zoom out one level), or add to step 3: 'Close the legend and click the green land in Florida' / 'Cierra la leyenda y haz clic en la tierra verde de Florida'.

findings.where: Latin American independence and US recognition labels at the Latin America in 1825 bookmark (q4-latin); Q4 'New nations and the Monroe Doctrine' steps 3 and 4
findings.what: Each symbol has a year: 'Mexico 1821', 'Republic of Colombia 1819'. Nothing on the map or the sheet says that's the year of independence, and the question is about comparing years with 1823. 'Paraguay 1811' is printed beside a blue circle (Brazil's, whose label is hidden), while Paraguay itself is an orange diamond. The 1800 boundaries layer also prints 'Perú' over the south, while 'Peru 1821' sits up by the coast. (So the map does have some place names, despite what the sheet says.)
findings.why: My students will compare the label years with 1823 instead of opening the pop-ups. They'll count Paraguay as recognized, and two Perus will confuse Spanish speakers in particular.
findings.suggestion: Change the labels to 'Mexico (independent 1821)' or drop the year, and add a line to both sheets: 'The year on the label is independence, not recognition' / 'El año de la etiqueta es la independencia, no el reconocimiento'. Fix label placement so each label stays next to its own symbol (and Brazil's shows), and turn off the 1800 boundary labels at this bookmark.
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q4-latin.png

findings.where: Latin American independence and US recognition pop-up (q4-circle); Q4 steps 3 and 4 (compare each recognition date with December 2, 1823)
findings.what: The same pop-up writes independence as '9 July 1816' and recognition as '1/27/1823, 12:00 AM'. Comparing with 2 de diciembre de 1823 is the whole task, and my students schooled in Latin America write the day first; a date like 8/4/1824 (Central America) they'd read as 8 April. 'Minister Plenipotentiary' adds a hard word the question doesn't need.
findings.why: The answer depends on reading these dates correctly, and the number format is the one my students are least sure of.
findings.suggestion: Format the recognition date in the pop-up as 'January 27, 1823', with no time, to match the independence line. Drop or simplify the Minister Plenipotentiary sentence.

findings.where: Land Spain gave up in 1819 pop-up, East Florida (q3-florida); Q3 'What did the United States gain from Spain?'
findings.what: The note says the Americans 'did agree to assume $5 million in damage caused by American citizens when they rebelled against Spain'. I can't make sense of it, my students will translate 'assume' and 'damage' word for word, and the sentence has no final period. I'd also check the fact: my understanding, and the answer notes', is that the United States agreed to pay its own citizens' claims against Spain, up to $5 million.
findings.why: A confusing sentence in the one pop-up that answers 'what did the US gain' leads my students to copy something they don't understand, and possibly something wrong.
findings.suggestion: After checking it against the treaty text, rewrite the note: 'The United States did not pay Spain for Florida. Instead, it agreed to pay up to $5 million that American citizens said Spain owed them.'
